The preceding subsections established the machinery by which cortical circuits compute self-supervised prediction errors (laminar and neuronal) and dynamically weight them according to inferred reliability (precision mechanisms). In the precision-weighting account, dopamine was characterized primarily as a gain modulator–setting effective precision Πl\Pi_l on prior and policy representations rather than carrying an instructive teaching signal per se. This characterization captures an important dimension of dopaminergic function at cortical targets, but it is incomplete in two respects. First, at cortical synapses, phasic dopamine (and, to varying degrees, other neuromodulators) also functions as a reinforcement-learning (RL) teaching signal that gates the consolidation of local Hebbian coincidences into lasting weight changes via three-factor plasticity rules–the "neuromodulator-gated (3-factor)" update rules listed in Table 1 for cortex and elaborated on in "The Fundamentals" and the upcoming section, "Cortical Plasticity" 1, 2. Second, the cortex itself generates a rich repertoire of reward- and outcome-related error signals–computed within cortical circuits by cortical neurons–that are distinct from both the self-supervised prediction errors of the laminar hierarchy and the phasic dopaminergic reward prediction errors (RPEs) classically associated with the basal ganglia. This subsection examines RL-related error signals as they are generated within and act upon cortical circuits, completing the cortical error-signal inventory before turning to the plasticity mechanisms that translate these signals into weight changes. The full treatment of the basal ganglia RL optimizer is deferred to its dedicated section ("The Basal Ganglia: Reinforcement Learning"); the molecular and biophysical details of three-factor plasticity are deferred to "Cortical Plasticity" and the "Synaptic Plasticity" subsection of "The Fundamentals".

Cortex does not merely receive RL error signals from subcortical sources; it computes its own error signals related to reward, outcome, and action evaluation—signals that operate alongside, and in some cases upstream of, the midbrain dopaminergic RPE system. The best-characterized cortical locus for outcome-related error computation is the medial frontal cortex, particularly the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and adjacent medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). Single-neuron recordings in macaque dACC have revealed cells whose firing rates scale with the magnitude of reward prediction errors—including, critically, both positive and negative surprises—producing unsigned outcome prediction errors that signal "how unexpected was this outcome?" rather than "was this outcome better or worse than expected?" 3, 4. These unsigned error signals are computationally significant because they can drive model updating and attentional reorientation without requiring access to the signed RPE that indexes value: detecting that an outcome was surprising, regardless of valence, is sufficient to signal that the current environmental model is inaccurate and should be revised 5. Consistent with this, human neuroimaging evidence supports a role for dACC in tracking environmental volatility—the rate at which reward contingencies change—and using this estimate to adjust learning rates, a meta-learning computation that operates on outcome prediction errors rather than raw reward magnitudes 5. Recent single-neuron recordings in both macaque and human medial frontal cortex have identified specific error-responsive neurons that are the likely generators of the error-related negativity (ERN), a scalp-recorded event-related potential that peaks∼\sim50-100ms after an erroneous response and is one of the most robust electrophysiological biomarkers of performance monitoring 6, 7. These error neurons respond to self-generated behavioral errors–a conjunction of intended action and actual outcome that constitutes a cortically computed action-outcome prediction error, generated within the medial frontal cortex’s own circuitry rather than being simply inherited from dopaminergic afferents; moreover, the discovery of homologous error neurons in macaque supplementary eye field and anterior cingulate cortex that are the direct generators of the ERN/error-related negativity provides a single-neuron-resolution bridge between the human scalp-recorded signal and the underlying cortical microcircuitry 8. The relationship between these cortically generated error signals and the midbrain RPE has been debated: the influential RL–ERN theory proposed that the ERN reflects the impact of a phasic dopaminergic negative RPE on ACC 9, but the single-neuron evidence now makes clear that ACC possesses its own error-computing machinery–neurons that fire to errors regardless of whether the error entails a reward loss, an incorrect motor response, or a violated temporal prediction–suggesting that ACC error signals are at least partly generated by a cortical action–outcome prediction mechanism rather than being passively inscribed by ascending dopamine 10, but the single-neuron evidence now makes clear that ACC possesses its own error-computing machinery–neurons that fire to errors regardless of whether the error entails a reward loss, an incorrect motor response, or a violated temporal prediction—suggesting that ACC error signals are at least partly generated by a cortical action-outcome prediction mechanism rather than being passively inscribed by ascending dopamine 8. The Alexander and Brown PRO (Predicted Response-Outcome) model formalizes this by proposing that mPFC learns to predict the probability and timing of each possible outcome given each possible action; surprise arises when an expected outcome fails to occur or an unexpected outcome occurs, generating both positive and negative outcome prediction errors that account for a wide range of ACC phenomena–including the ERN, the N2, feedback-related negativity, and reward positivity–within a single predictive-coding framework applied to the action-outcome domain 11. A primate study examines diverse value estimates in anterior cingulate cortex (Figure) 37. The study examines asymmetric prediction-error responses (Figure).

A second cortical region contributing essential components to the RL error computation is the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Unlike dACC, OFC does not primarily encode outcome prediction errors per se; rather, it maintains detailed representations of expected outcomes—including their sensory-specific identity, magnitude, and probability—that serve as the predictions against which actual outcomes are compared by downstream evaluative circuits 12. These representations are transmitted to midbrain dopamine neurons, where they become a critical input to the RPE computation. The causal evidence is direct: OFC lesions degrade the ability of dopamine neurons to signal expectancy-related changes in firing, reducing RPE signals as if the predictions required to compute them had been lost or degraded 13. This positions OFC not as an error-computing area but as a prediction-generating area whose outputs are essential ingredients of the RL error signal—formally analogous to the role that deep-layer (L5/6) prediction-generating populations play in the self-supervised predictive-coding hierarchy, but specialized for the value and outcome domain. Similarly, recent intracranial recordings in humans during a probabilistic learning task have demonstrated that reward and punishment learning engage overlapping frontal cortical territories—including prefrontal and insular regions—but rely on dissociable inter-regional interaction patterns 14. These cortically generated signals–unsigned outcome prediction errors in dACC, outcome predictions in OFC, volatility estimates that modulate learning rate, spectrally multiplexed reward and punishment signals across frontal cortex–converge on a critical cortical function: the cortex provides the belief-state representations and outcome predictions that make subcortical RPE computation possible under real-world conditions of ambiguity and partial observability. In environments where the hidden state must be inferred (partially observable tasks), a simple comparison of received reward against a cached expected value is insufficient; the agent must first infer which state it occupies, then compute the RPE conditional on that inferred state. This computation requires cortical input. Inactivation of rodent mPFC disrupts dopaminergic RPE signals specifically in tasks where the hidden state must be inferred from a history of observations, but not in tasks where the state is directly observable; computational modeling localizes this effect to a circuit in which mPFC furnishes the posterior belief over hidden states to the dopamine system, which uses this belief as the basis for computing the RPE 15. Whole-brain viral tracing studies have confirmed that VTA dopamine neurons receive convergent monosynaptic and polysynaptic inputs from a wide array of cortical areas—including prefrontal, orbitofrontal, insular, and cingulate cortices—providing the anatomical substrate for this cortex-to-midbrain flow of state and value information 16. The assembled picture is that the RPE signal broadcast by dopamine neurons is not computed in isolation by the midbrain but is a distributed computation to which cortex contributes the highest-dimensional inputs–inferred state, expected outcome identity, volatility-modulated learning rate–and from which cortex receives the compressed, low-bandwidth teaching signal in return.

This cortex->midbrain->cortex teaching loop defines the channel through which RL error signals act back on cortical synapses. The return arm of the loop—phasic dopamine broadcast from VTA/SNc to cortex—is the third factor in the three-factor plasticity rule referenced in Table 1 and the "Synaptic Plasticity" section of "The Fundamentals". Importantly, this dopaminergic return projection is not spatially uniform across the cortical mantle. The density of dopaminergic innervation follows a pronounced gradient: frontal, premotor, and primary motor cortices receive the densest dopaminergic fiber plexuses; anterior cingulate, insular, and entorhinal cortices are moderately innervated; and posterior sensory cortices–including primary visual, auditory, and somatosensory areas–receive comparatively sparse projections (see next section "Cortical Plasticity" for greater detail) 17, 18. Within the heavily innervated frontal and motor territories, dopaminergic fibers further exhibit laminar specificity: in prefrontal cortex, the densest fiber plexuses occupy layers I-III and again layers V/VI–the same deep-layer compartment hosting the prediction-generating pyramidal neurons of the laminar hierarchy–while in primary motor and premotor cortex, a prominent projection targets layer I and the deep corticospinal output layers 19, 20. This innervation gradient is functionally interpretable through the RL teaching-signal framework developed above. Frontal and motor cortices sit at the policy-output end (or "decision-making" end) of the cortical hierarchy: prefrontal areas convert inferred goals and contextual beliefs into abstract action plans; premotor and motor areas convert those plans into concrete movement commands. These territories are precisely where reward-related teaching signals are most needed, because the core problem that RL must solve–credit assignment to the internal representations that generated rewarded or punished actions–requires that the teaching signal reach the synapses encoding the state-to-action mapping. Dense dopaminergic innervation concentrates the third factor at cortical sites where policy is computed and motor programs are specified, ensuring that eligibility traces at policy-relevant synapses have a high probability of encountering a phasic DA transient within their decay window τe\tau_e. Posterior sensory areas, by contrast, can rely primarily on the self-supervised prediction errors of the laminar hierarchy for representational learning–their perceptual representations are shaped predominantly by the predictive-coding error signals described in the preceding subsections–consistent with their sparser dopaminergic innervation. Dopamine still plays a role in these sensory territories (e.g., attentional gain modulation, reward-modulated perceptual learning), but that role is subsidiary rather than dominant 21, 22. The heterogeneity of dopaminergic innervation thus determines not whether a cortical region can learn, but the relative weighting of self-supervised versus reinforcement-driven learning at each point in the hierarchy. At each cortical synapse, the local Hebbian coincidence between presynaptic activity and postsynaptic depolarization does not directly produce a lasting weight change; instead, it sets a transient eligibility trace eij(t)e_{ij}(t)—a molecular flag, likely involving calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase and related signaling cascades, which marks the synapse as a candidate for modification 2. The trace decays exponentially with characteristic time constant τe\tau_e unless a neuromodulatory signal (the "third factor") arrives within the eligibility window, at which point the trace is converted into a lasting change in synaptic efficacy. The critical parameter for cortical RL is the eligibility-trace time constant τe\tau_e. In dorsal and ventral striatum, τe\tau_e has been measured at∼\sim0.3-1s 23, 24; in visual and frontal cortex, eligibility traces for both LTP and LTD have been demonstrated with substantially longer time constants on the order of∼\sim5-10s 25, 2, and hippocampal traces may extend to minutes 26, 2, 27. These longer cortical trace durations are computationally significant: they extend the temporal window over which a delayed RL teaching signal can retroactively modify the synapses that were active at the time of a decision, bridging the gap between action and outcome characteristic of naturalistic behavior.

The teaching role of phasic dopamine at cortical synapses is not in conflict with its precision-modulating role described above; the two functions are largely segregated by temporal dynamics and circuit locus. Tonic dopamine–the slowly fluctuating baseline concentration set by irregular, population-level VTA/SNc firing–modulates the gain and dynamic stability of cortical representations through sustained D1 and D2 receptor occupancy, implementing the precision function described in the "Neuromodulators as Precision-Weighting Machinery" subsection: setting attractor depth in PFC, biasing the exploitation-exploration trade-off, and tuning policy commitment (the γ\gamma parameter in the active-inference formalism) 28, 29. Phasic dopamine–the brief (~100-500ms), high-amplitude transient elicited by unexpected reward or reward-predicting cues–drives a rapid, spatially broad surge in DA concentration that acts on the eligibility-trace mechanism to convert recently flagged synaptic coincidences into durable weight changes. In active inference terms, tonic DA sets the precision (confidence) assigned to current policies, while phasic DA updates the generative model’s parameters–state-transition probabilities, outcome predictions–in light of new evidence about reward contingencies 30. The distinction is not absolute: tonic and phasic signals are superimposed on the same axonal arbors and act on overlapping receptor populations, with functional outcomes depending on receptor affinity, local reuptake kinetics, and the recent history of DA release. But the separation by timescale is sufficient to support dual use of a single neuromodulatory channel for both precision control and teaching. A 2025 study examines adolescent mouse frontal-cortex plasticity (Figure) 40. The study manipulates dopamine-receptor signaling (Figure).

This dual identity connects directly to the dendritic error-computation framework developed in "Neuronal Error Signals." Urbanczik and Senn explicitly demonstrated that their dendritic prediction-error rule—in which synaptic plasticity is driven by the mismatch between somatic spiking and dendritic prediction—subsumes RL as a special case: when the plasticity induction variable A related preprint models cellular and dendritic specialization (Figure) 41. Sacramento et al.’s three-compartment extension preserves this property: the apical voltage deflection that encodes hierarchical credit-assignment error can be conjunctively gated by a neuromodulatory signal arriving at the same dendritic domain (e.g. via dopamine receptors expressed on apical dendrites of deep-layer pyramidal neurons), so that the direction of the weight change is set by the local dendritic mismatch and the magnitude (and whether it is consolidated at all) is scaled by reward-related feedback 32. Viewed this way, the RL teaching signal does not introduce a fundamentally new error-computation circuit into cortex; rather, it modulates the gain and consolidation of the same dendritic mismatch signals that already drive self-supervised learning. Phasic DA acts as a multiplicative gate that converts "this synapse contributed to the current error" (the eligibility trace set by the dendritic comparator) into "this synapse contributed to the error and the outcome was better (or worse) than expected" (the consolidated weight change). The three-factor rule is therefore best understood not as a separate RL mechanism operating in parallel with the predictive-coding error architecture, but as a neuromodulatory elaboration of the same dendritic error-computation substrate—one that allows cortical plasticity to be shaped by outcome and reward signals without requiring the cortex to abandon its local, self-supervised learning logic and, ultimately, to consolidate state-action contingencies that improve expected outcomes under a preference distribution 33, 34.

Alexander and Brown’s Hierarchical Error Representation (HER) model makes this integration fully explicit, demonstrating that a stack of cortical predictive-coding modules–each predicting the expected timing and identity of the next action-outcome contingency at a given level of abstraction–naturally gives rise to hierarchically organized error signals that encompass both sensory prediction errors (the domain of self-supervised cortical learning) and action-outcome prediction errors (the domain of RL), without requiring fundamentally different computational principles at any level 35. In the HER model, each level of the medial and lateral PFC hierarchy learns to predict the probability and timing of outcomes conditional on actions at that level of abstraction; prediction failures propagate as error signals that drive both belief updating (analogous to perceptual inference) and policy updating (analogous to RL). The model reproduces a wide array of empirical phenomena across both lateral PFC (rule encoding, task switching, error-likelihood effects) and medial PFC (ERN, feedback-related negativity, N2, reward positivity), suggesting that the cortical RL error signals observed in ACC and mPFC need not arise from a dedicated RL subsystem embedded within cortex but instead emerge naturally from the same predictive architecture applied to action–outcome contingencies rather than—or in addition to—sensory state transitions. This resonates with the active predictive coding (APC) framework discussed in "Laminar Error Signals": APC posits that every cortical area maintains both a state-transition network and a policy network, with action prediction errors operating alongside state prediction errors as canonical columnar error signals 36. The HER model can be read as the RL-facing interpretation of this same principle: wherever cortex predicts the consequences of actions, it automatically generates action-outcome error signals that support reinforcement-like learning within the self-supervised architecture. A 2026 model compares error-neuron microcircuits with predictive-coding networks (Figure) 42.

In synthesis, the cortical error-signal repertoire extends beyond the self-supervised prediction errors and precision weights developed in the preceding subsections to encompass a family of RL-related signals: cortically generated unsigned outcome prediction errors (dACC/mPFC), expected-outcome representations that are necessary inputs to the subcortical RPE computation (OFC), reward and punishment error signals across frontal cortex, belief-state inferences that determine the content of the dopaminergic RPE under partial observability (mPFC->VTA), and the phasic dopaminergic teaching signal that returns to cortex to gate synaptic consolidation via eligibility traces. Moreover, the density of dopaminergic innervation is itself spatially graded—heaviest at the frontal and motor policy-output territories, lightest in posterior sensory cortex—so that the relative influence of RL-gated versus self-supervised plasticity shifts systematically across the cortical hierarchy. The key architectural insight—and the reason these signals belong in a section on cortical error signals rather than being deferred entirely to the basal ganglia—is that they do not constitute a separate "RL module" grafted onto the cortical sheet. Rather, they are deeply intertwined with the self-supervised predictive architecture: the same laminar circuits that generate sensory prediction errors also generate outcome prediction errors (via the same predictive logic applied to action–outcome contingencies); the same dendritic compartmentalization that implements local credit assignment also supports three-factor gating by neuromodulatory third factors; and the eligibility-trace mechanism bridges these two regimes by allowing delayed reward signals to retroactively sculpt synapses whose Hebbian coincidences were flagged by the fast, self-supervised error-computation machinery. The result is a cortex in which self-supervised and reinforcement error signals share a common computational substrate and are distinguished primarily by the timescale and source of the teaching signal—immediate local mismatch for self-supervised updating, delayed neuromodulatory broadcast for RL—rather than by fundamentally different circuitry. The mechanisms by which cortical synapses implement this shared substrate—the molecular identity of eligibility traces, the receptor cascades activated by each neuromodulator, and the metaplastic rules governing the interaction between self-supervised and RL-driven weight modifications—are the subject of the next section.
